major_issues: (1) Potential circularity with respect to how immune-rich neighborhoods were initially characterized in the exploration log: if immune hotspots or interfaces were defined using similar interferon/immune signatures, then testing for higher interferon and checkpoint activity in immune-adjacent tumor spots risks re-demonstrating the same signal. (2) Confounding by local sequencing depth and complexity: the test_plan mentions optional adjustment for total_counts and n_genes_by_counts, but immune-rich regions and tumor–stroma interfaces may systematically differ in QC metrics or tissue coverage; not including these as default covariates could bias results. (3) Dependence on somewhat vague definitions of "immune-classified" spots and adjacency: while Classification categories exist (e.g., Lymphocytes, Invasive cancer + lymphocytes), it is not fully specified whether mixed classes are treated as immune neighbors or tumor, and how k and distance thresholds will be chosen and justified. (4) Single-sample limitation: enrichment of immune-activated tumor spots near immune neighborhoods could reflect idiosyncratic sample-specific architecture; while this is acceptable for this dataset, generalizability should not be over-interpreted.
minor_issues: (1) The statement focuses on "interferon response and immune checkpoint program activity" but the test_plan expands to include antigen-presentation programs; clarifying in the statement that antigen presentation is also of interest would tighten alignment. (2) The phrase "for example k = 6 within a fixed spatial radius" leaves ambiguity about whether kNN is within a radius or a pure kNN graph; pre-specifying one approach would reduce flexibility. (3) The neighborhood enrichment portion of the test_plan partially overlaps conceptually with the primary comparison, and could be simplified or more clearly separated as a secondary analysis. (4) It is not explicit whether artefact or NaN-classified spots are removed before constructing neighborhoods; this should be stated to avoid accidental inclusion of non-tissue regions.
suggested_refinements: (1) Explicitly define immune-classified neighbor categories (e.g., Lymphocytes plus Invasive cancer + lymphocytes as immune-rich) and fix adjacency parameters a priori (e.g., 6 nearest neighbors in the Visium grid without an additional radius constraint). (2) Make adjustment for total_counts and n_genes_by_counts a default part of the primary linear model, and consider including a binary indicator for low-coverage spots or distance-to-array-edge as additional covariates to mitigate edge and coverage effects. (3) Clarify in the hypothesis statement that antigen-presentation programs are included, or in the test_plan restrict to the two named programs. (4) To reduce circularity, ensure that the immune-adjacent vs immune-distant tumor grouping is defined strictly from the Classification labels and spatial proximity, without using interferon or checkpoint expression in that definition, and note this explicitly in the plan. (5) Optionally predefine gene sets from external references (e.g., MSigDB Hallmark interferon alpha/gamma, curated checkpoint and antigen-presentation genes) so that module scoring does not involve post-hoc gene selection from this dataset.

major_issues: (1) Possible dependence on already observed core-versus-edge differences: OBSERVATION_012 and CV2 already highlight radial heterogeneity with invasion markers at edges and proliferation in cores; the current hypothesis largely formalizes this pattern, so care is needed to avoid re-testing a pattern that was used to motivate the gene programs and distance-based grouping. (2) Confounding by global spatial trends and QC: distance from non-tumor tissue may be correlated with array coordinates, local tissue thickness, or sequencing depth. While generalized additive models are mentioned as optional, lack of mandatory QC and spatial covariates in the primary models could inflate associations. (3) Ambiguity in the operational definition of "tumor-classified" versus "non-tumor" categories when using the mixed class "Invasive cancer + lymphocytes" and DCIS; different choices here could materially change the computed distances and group assignments. (4) Limited dynamic range of distances in a single, modestly sized tumor region may reduce power to detect smooth gradients, especially if the tumor area is small or irregular; this should be acknowledged in feasibility expectations.
minor_issues: (1) The statement speaks of "opposing spatial gradients" but does not specify whether evidence for monotonicity (e.g., strictly increasing or decreasing trends) is required or whether simple edge-vs-core contrasts suffice; clarifying this would aid interpretation. (2) The test_plan suggests both continuous and discretized distance analyses; pre-specifying the primary approach (e.g., continuous models with a secondary categorical analysis) would avoid analytic flexibility. (3) The gene set descriptions (e.g., "vimentin, matrix metalloproteinases, integrins, TGF-beta pathway targets") are informal; referencing a concrete external source (e.g., Hallmark EMT, REACTOME cell cycle) would improve reproducibility. (4) There is no explicit plan for handling class imbalance if the number of core versus edge tumor spots differs substantially; power and variance estimates could be discussed.
suggested_refinements: (1) Predefine "tumor-classified" as the union of specific Classification categories (e.g., Invasive cancer + lymphocytes and DCIS) and "non-tumor" as Normal + stroma + lymphocytes, Stroma, and Stroma + adipose, and document this explicitly in the test_plan. (2) Specify distance from non-tumor tissue as the minimum Euclidean distance in obsm['spatial'] measured in the native pixel units, and fix whether the primary analysis uses continuous distance (with Spearman/linear models) or discretized tertiles. (3) Make inclusion of total_counts, n_genes_by_counts, and optionally smooth functions of spatial coordinates mandatory covariates in the primary regression models to reduce confounding by QC and global spatial trends. (4) Use externally curated EMT and proliferation gene sets (e.g., MSigDB Hallmark EMT, Hallmark G2M checkpoint, Hallmark E2F targets) restricted to genes present in the dataset, instead of ad hoc marker lists. (5) Define a minimal effect size of interest (e.g., difference in module score between edge and core) and ensure that group sizes based on the data inventory provide reasonable power; note explicitly that results will be interpreted cautiously if gradients are weak or distances have narrow range.

major_issues: (1) Potential circularity relative to OBSERVATION_013: the exploration log already notes ECM-rich stromal regions near tumor borders based on similar expression patterns; testing for higher CAF/ECM module scores in peritumoral stroma may risk re-demonstrating the exploratory finding unless care is taken to separate how peritumoral regions were defined from the ECM expression patterns used to label them. (2) Dependence on an imprecise definition of "stromal or fibroblast-rich non-epithelial, non-immune spots": Classification categories (Stroma, Stroma + adipose tissue, Normal + stroma + lymphocytes) mix stromal and other components, and the test_plan does not fully specify whether mixed classes are included or how lymphocyte-enriched normal stroma will be handled. (3) Peritumoral vs distant stroma definitions may be sensitive to the choice of k and radius; without fixing these a priori or conducting sensitivity analyses, results could be somewhat arbitrary. (4) QC and tissue-coverage confounding: peritumoral stroma might systematically differ in nCount_RNA, nFeature_RNA, or distance to array edges, and although QC covariates are mentioned as optional, they should likely be mandatory to strengthen causal interpretation. (5) Spatial autocorrelation tests (global and local Moran's I) assume a specified neighbor graph; the plan mentions a "Visium grid" but does not state whether adjacency is based on array_row/array_col or spatial coordinates, which could affect hotspot detection.
minor_issues: (1) The hypothesis statement combines two somewhat distinct claims: higher CAF/ECM activity near tumor and spatial autocorrelation/hotspot formation. These could be separated into primary and secondary components to avoid overloading a single hypothesis. (2) The list of example genes (collagens, fibronectin, MMPs, LOX, ACTA2) is reasonable but not formally linked to a specific gene set resource; this may introduce subjectivity in module scoring. (3) It is not specified how "distant" stroma will be operationally defined beyond not meeting adjacency criteria; adding a minimum distance threshold or sensitivity checks would clarify. (4) Artefact and NaN spots are not explicitly excluded when building neighbor graphs or computing distances. (5) The plan does not mention handling of multiple stromal subtypes that might cluster in different spatial regions independent of tumor proximity (e.g., adipose-rich stroma), which could complicate interpretation of ECM gradients.
suggested_refinements: (1) Explicitly define stromal categories to include (e.g., Stroma and Stroma + adipose tissue, optionally Normal + stroma + lymphocytes with an added control for lymphocyte proportion if estimable) and clearly exclude immune-only and artefact/NaN spots. (2) Fix peritumoral stroma as stromal spots whose 6 nearest spatial neighbors include at least one tumor-classified spot, and define distant stroma as stromal spots with no tumor neighbor within a specified Euclidean distance threshold; document chosen parameters and consider a brief sensitivity analysis in the analysis plan. (3) Make adjustment for total_counts and n_genes_by_counts a core part of the regression models comparing peritumoral and distant stroma, and consider including distance to array edge or local spot density as additional covariates. (4) Separate the hypothesis into two tiers: a primary claim about elevated CAF/ECM module scores in peritumoral versus distant stroma, and a secondary claim about positive spatial autocorrelation and hotspot enrichment near tumor, each with its own explicit success criteria. (5) Use curated ECM/CAF gene sets from external resources (e.g., NABA extracellular matrix, published CAF signatures) intersected with genes detected in this dataset, to avoid post-hoc marker selection from the same data.
